milestones.title: utility

functions.name: utility

milestones.task: Write utility(src, instances, fuel_budget=FUEL). Compile src with a fresh Fuel. Wrap the function in a checker that rejects any return value that is not a finite int or float. Pack every instance. Return minus the mean bin count, or PENALTY on any failure.
milestones.checkpoint: check.py verifies: hand-worked values (-2.0, -3.0) and best fit. Seven kinds of failure must all give exactly PENALTY. They are a syntax error, an import, an endless loop, division by zero, a boolean, an infinity from repeated squaring and a wrong signature. The same short loop must be fine with 10,000 fuel and a penalty with 20.
hints: A fresh Fuel(fuel_budget) per call. Fuel is shared across all the instances of one call, so a slow program runs out over the whole set.
Check the type with type(v) not in (int, float). Do not use isinstance, because bool is a subclass of int.
Put math.isfinite(v) in the same check, so nan and infinity are caught.
Catch Exception around both the compile step and the packing. One broad clause is fine here, because every failure maps to the same penalty.
milestones.solution:
def utility(src, instances, fuel_budget=FUEL):
    """Minus the mean bins, or PENALTY on any failure."""
    fuel = Fuel(fuel_budget)
    try:
        fn = compile_restricted(src, fuel)
    except Exception:
        return PENALTY

    def checked(item, rem):
        v = fn(float(item), float(rem))
        if type(v) not in (int, float) or not math.isfinite(v):
            raise ValueError("bad priority value")
        return v

    try:
        counts = [pack(items, checked) for items in instances]
    except Exception:                 # OutOfFuel, ValueError, ZeroDivisionError, ...
        return PENALTY
    return -sum(counts) / len(counts)
milestones.explain:
Every level above this one needs one number per heuristic. That number must exist for every candidate, including broken ones. A search that crashes on its first bad program is not a search. So utility must never raise.

The sandbox from lab 3 is given. compile_restricted turns text into a function that can only call abs, min and max. It also counts fuel: one tick per function call and per loop pass. pack(items, priority) runs online bin packing. You combine them.

Take the instance [60, 60, 40, 40] and first fit (return 0). The first 60 opens bin 1, which has 40 left. The second 60 does not fit there, so it opens bin 2. The first 40 goes into bin 1, the second 40 into bin 2. That is two bins, so the utility is -2.0. Averages over instances work the same way: two instances needing 2 and 4 bins give -3.0.

Anything that goes wrong gets PENALTY, which is -1000.0. That is far below any real score, so a failing program can never win a comparison. Failures come in four kinds. The program may be rejected. It may run out of fuel, as an endless loop does. It may raise an exception, such as division by zero. Or it may return something other than a finite number, such as a boolean, nan or infinity. A boolean deserves care. In Python True == 1, so a program returning item > 3 would run without error and mean nothing.
milestones.card:
A search needs one number for every program it tries, including broken ones. A search that crashes on its first bad program is not a search, so utility must never raise. A working program scores minus its mean bin count, so higher is better. Anything that goes wrong scores PENALTY (-1000), far below any real score, so a failing program can never win a comparison.

Compile with compile_restricted(src, Fuel(fuel_budget)): one fresh Fuel for the whole call, shared by all instances, so an endless loop ends in OutOfFuel. Wrap the compiled function in a checker that rejects any return value that is not a finite int or float. Test type(v) in (int, float): in Python True == 1, so a program returning item > 3 would run without error and mean nothing. Run pack(items, checker) on every instance, and turn every failure, whatever its kind, into PENALTY.

[60, 60, 40, 40] with priority always 0: bins [60, 40] and [60, 40]
2 bins, utility -2.0; two instances needing 2 and 4 bins: -3.0

milestones.title: meta-utility

functions.name: meta_utility
functions.signature: def meta_utility(config, task_seeds, budget, lo=20, hi=60):
functions.doc:
The mean utility of what the evolver finds, over several tasks.

For each task seed t (in the order given):
  * the search instances are make_instances([1000*t + j for j in range(N_SEARCH)], ITEMS, lo, hi)
  * the scoring instances are  make_instances([1000*t + 500 + j for j in range(N_EVAL)], ITEMS, lo, hi)
    (the evolver never sees these)
  * make a fresh Budget(budget), run evolve(config, search, counter, random.Random(t)),
    and take utility(found, scoring instances).
Return the mean over tasks. The same arguments must always give the same number.

milestones.task: Write meta_utility(config, task_seeds, budget, lo=20, hi=60). For each task seed, build the search and scoring instances, make a fresh Budget(budget), call evolve(config, search, counter, random.Random(t)), and score the result on the scoring instances with utility. Return the mean.
milestones.checkpoint: check.py verifies: the answer is deterministic. It equals the mean of the single-task answers. With budget 1 it equals the seed's utility on the scoring instances. Three tasks create three Budget counters that each run to 21 (budget 20 plus the refused request). The scoring instances are used once per task. And lo and hi reach the instances.
hints: make_instances(seeds, ITEMS, lo, hi) builds a list of instances. Pass lo and hi through, because milestone 5 changes them.
Create Budget(budget) inside the loop over tasks, not before it.
You do not need to catch BudgetExceeded. The given evolve catches it and returns the best program found so far.
milestones.solution:
def meta_utility(config, task_seeds, budget, lo=20, hi=60):
    """Mean utility of what the evolver finds."""
    total = 0.0
    for t in task_seeds:
        search = make_instances([1000 * t + j for j in range(N_SEARCH)], ITEMS, lo, hi)
        scoring = make_instances([1000 * t + 500 + j for j in range(N_EVAL)], ITEMS, lo, hi)
        counter = Budget(budget)
        found = evolve(config, search, counter, random.Random(t))
        total += utility(found, scoring)
    return total / len(task_seeds)
milestones.explain:
Now the step up. Given a config, how good is it? You cannot ask the config. You have to run the evolver with it and look at what comes out. That is meta_utility.

Three rules make the number fair. First, the budget is fixed. Every config gets the same number of heuristic evaluations, so a config cannot win by simply running longer. Second, each task gets its own fresh Budget. A shared counter would let the first task use it all and starve the rest. Third, the found heuristic is scored on instances the evolver never saw. Otherwise the config that overfits its search instances looks best.

For task seed t, the search instances use seeds 1000*t + j, and the scoring instances use seeds 1000*t + 500 + j. The evolver's own random stream is random.Random(t). So the same config on the same tasks always gives the same number. The result is the mean over tasks.

A budget of 1 is a useful anchor. The evolver can then score only the seed program, so the meta-utility is the seed's utility, whatever the config. The next table shows what a bigger budget buys. It is the script below run on the training tasks:

import sys
sys.path.insert(0, ".")
import solution as lab

tasks = lab.TRAIN_TASKS
print(f"{'budget':>6} {'naive':>8} {'tuned':>8}")
for budget in (1, 5, 20, 60):
    a = lab.meta_utility(lab.DEFAULT, tasks, budget)
    b = lab.meta_utility(lab.TUNED, tasks, budget)
    print(f"{budget:>6} {a:8.3f} {b:8.3f}")
budget    naive    tuned
     1  -36.722  -36.722
     5  -36.722  -35.944
    20  -36.722  -35.778
    60  -36.722  -35.944

Read the table carefully. The naive config never moves, because it cannot make the edit it needs. The tuned config gains about 0.8 to 0.9 bins from a budget of 5 on, and then does not improve with a larger budget. It even drifts a little at 60, because the evolver picks the winner on only three search instances and the scoring instances are different. That is a small version of the problem milestone 5 measures.
milestones.card:
Given a config (the settings of the evolver, the search that writes heuristics), how good is it? You cannot ask the config. You run the evolver with it and look at what comes out. Three rules make the number fair. The budget is fixed, so a config cannot win by running longer. Each task gets a fresh Budget, because a shared counter would let the first task use it all. And the heuristic found is scored on instances the evolver never saw, or a config that overfits its search instances would look best.

For each task seed t, build the search instances from seeds 1000*t + j and the scoring instances from 1000*t + 500 + j with make_instances (counts N_SEARCH and N_EVAL, sizes lo and hi). Run evolve(config, search, counter, random.Random(t)), then take utility of what it returns on the scoring instances. Return the mean over tasks. The same arguments must always give the same number.

budget = 1: the evolver can score only the seed program,
so every config gets the seed's utility on the scoring instances

milestones.title: the seed improver

functions.name: improve
functions.signature: def improve(config, score, rng, rounds, settings=SEED_SETTINGS):
functions.doc:
Hill-climb over configs. Return (best_config, best_score).

Start with best = config and best_score = score(config). Then, for each of `rounds`
rounds, make settings.proposals candidates with
perturb(best, CHOICES, rng, settings.n_change, settings.step) (draw them all before scoring
any), and score them in order. Whenever a candidate scores STRICTLY higher than the best so
far, it becomes the best. Return the best. The number of score calls is
1 + rounds * proposals.

milestones.task: Write improve(config, score, rng, rounds, settings=SEED_SETTINGS). It returns (best_config, best_score). Draw the candidates with perturb(best, CHOICES, rng, settings.n_change, settings.step).
milestones.checkpoint: check.py verifies: the exact sequence of configs scored matches a reference. The number of score calls is 1 + rounds * proposals. A constant score returns the start unchanged. And on the real scorer the naive config improves. The check prints the gain.
hints: Call score(config) once before the loop and keep the result. Do not call it again for the best config at the start of every round.
Build the round's candidates with a list comprehension first. Then loop over that list to score them.
Compare with >, not >=. If a candidate ties, the earlier config stays.
The returned score must be the score of the returned config. Update both together.
milestones.solution:
def improve(config, score, rng, rounds, settings=SEED_SETTINGS):
    """Hill-climb over configs."""
    best = config
    best_score = score(config)
    for _ in range(rounds):
        candidates = [perturb(best, CHOICES, rng, settings.n_change, settings.step)
                      for _ in range(settings.proposals)]
        for cand in candidates:
            s = score(cand)
            if s > best_score:
                best, best_score = cand, s
    return best, best_score
milestones.explain:
With a meta-utility you can search over configs. The simplest search is hill climbing: change something, keep the change if the score rises, and otherwise drop it. The improver does this on a Config.

The improver has its own settings. They live in a small class called Settings. The field proposals says how many candidate configs it tries per round. The field n_change says how many config fields each candidate changes. The field step says how far along a field's list of choices a change moves. The given perturb(obj, choices, rng, n_change, step) makes one candidate. The seed settings are Settings(2, 1, 1): two proposals per round, one field changed, one step.

The order of work matters for reproducibility. Each round, draw all proposals candidates from the best config so far, and only then score them in order. A candidate replaces the best only if its score is strictly higher. A tie changes nothing. The total number of score calls is 1 + rounds * proposals: one for the start, then the proposals.

Here is a toy example you can check by hand. Take a made-up score, -|w_shape - 6|, and start at w_shape = 0. With step = 1 and one field changed, a candidate that picks w_shape is either 1 or 0. The value 1 scores -5, which beats -6. The other move is clamped at 0 and ties. So only upward moves are kept, and each round can gain at most one unit per accepted candidate.
milestones.card:
With a score for configs you can search over configs. The simplest search is hill climbing: change something, keep the change if the score rises, otherwise drop it. The improver does this on a Config, the evolver's settings. It has settings of its own, in a Settings record: proposals candidates per round, n_change fields changed per candidate, and step positions moved along a field's list of choices.

Start with best = config and its score. Each round, draw all settings.proposals candidates from the current best with the given perturb(best, CHOICES, rng, n_change, step), and only then score them in order. The checker replays the exact sequence of configs scored, so the order of drawing and scoring matters. A candidate replaces the best only if its score is strictly higher: a tie changes nothing. The score calls number 1 + rounds * proposals. Return (best_config, best_score).

score = -abs(w_shape - 6), start w_shape = 0, step 1:
a move to 1 scores -5 and wins; a move down clamps at 0, ties, and is dropped

milestones.title: self-application

functions.name: improver_utility
functions.signature: def improver_utility(settings, score, start=DEFAULT, seeds=IMPROVE_SEEDS, calls=CALLS):
functions.doc:
How good an improver is: the mean gain in `score` it makes from `start`.

For each seed s run improve(start, score, random.Random(s), rounds, settings) where
rounds = calls // settings.proposals (so every improver makes about the same number of
score calls: a fair fight). The gain of a run is best_score - score(start).
Return the mean gain over the seeds.

functions.name: self_improve
functions.signature: def self_improve(score, rng, rounds, settings=SEED_SETTINGS, start=DEFAULT):
functions.doc:
Improve the improver: hill-climb over Settings with improver_utility as the score.

Same shape as improve(): best = settings, best_u = improver_utility(settings, score, start);
for each of `rounds` rounds make ONE candidate with
perturb(best, SETTING_CHOICES, rng, 1, 1), compute its improver_utility, and keep it if STRICTLY
higher. Return (best_settings, best_u).

milestones.task: Write improver_utility(settings, score, start=DEFAULT, seeds=IMPROVE_SEEDS, calls=CALLS) and self_improve(score, rng, rounds, settings=SEED_SETTINGS, start=DEFAULT). Use rounds = calls // settings.proposals inside improver_utility.
milestones.checkpoint: check.py verifies: the mean gain matches a reference on a toy score. The number of score calls is the expected count; self_improve calls improver_utility exactly 1 + rounds times and keeps only strict improvements. And on the real training tasks the improved improver beats the seed improver. It also tests on twelve fresh random streams, which the self-improvement never saw.
hints: Compute score(start) once, before the loop over seeds.
Use random.Random(s) for each seed s, so every improver faces the same streams.
An improver with 6 proposals and calls=4 gets 0 rounds, and a gain of exactly 0. That is correct. Do not special-case it.
In self_improve, compute the start's improver_utility once, then compare each candidate with the best so far.
milestones.solution:
def improver_utility(settings, score, start=DEFAULT, seeds=IMPROVE_SEEDS, calls=CALLS):
    """Mean gain an improver makes from `start`."""
    rounds = calls // settings.proposals
    base = score(start)
    gains = []
    for s in seeds:
        _, best_score = improve(start, score, random.Random(s), rounds, settings)
        gains.append(best_score - base)
    return sum(gains) / len(gains)

def self_improve(score, rng, rounds, settings=SEED_SETTINGS, start=DEFAULT):
    """The same hill-climb, one level up."""
    best = settings
    best_u = improver_utility(settings, score, start)
    for _ in range(rounds):
        cand = perturb(best, SETTING_CHOICES, rng, 1, 1)
        u = improver_utility(cand, score, start)
        if u > best_u:
            best, best_u = cand, u
    return best, best_u
milestones.explain:
This is the step the lab is named for. The improver has settings. Settings are numbers. So you can improve the improver with the improver's own method.

To do that you need a score for an improver. Define it as the mean gain the improver makes from a fixed start config, over a few random streams. Run improve once per stream, and average best_score - score(start). This is a meta-meta-utility, and it is a number like any other.

One rule keeps the comparison fair. Every improver gets about the same number of score calls, CALLS = 4 rounds-times-proposals. An improver with 4 proposals runs 1 round, and one with 1 proposal runs 4. Without this rule, "more proposals" would always win, and you would learn only that compute helps.

Then self_improve hill-climbs over Settings exactly as improve hill-climbs over Config. It makes one candidate per round, with perturb(best, SETTING_CHOICES, rng, 1, 1), scores it with improver_utility, and keeps it only if strictly better.

What should you expect? The naive start config needs one specific fix: a positive weight on the w_shape edit. A seed improver changes one field per candidate, so it reaches that fix slowly. An improver that changes two or three fields at once reaches it faster. So the likely win for self-improvement is a larger n_change. That is a small, dull, true result.
milestones.card:
An improver (a hill climber over configs) has settings of its own, and settings are numbers, so you can improve the improver with its own method. That needs a score for an improver: the mean gain it makes from a fixed start config, over a few random streams. It is a number like any other, one level up.

improver_utility(settings, score, ...) computes score(start) once, runs improve once per seed with random.Random(s), and averages best_score minus that start score. For a fair fight every improver gets about the same number of score calls, so use rounds = calls // settings.proposals. Without that rule more proposals would always win, and you would learn only that compute helps. self_improve hill-climbs over Settings exactly as improve does over Config: one candidate per round, from perturb(best, SETTING_CHOICES, rng, 1, 1), scored by improver_utility and kept only if strictly better. That is 1 + rounds utility calls.

calls = 4: proposals 4 gives 1 round, proposals 2 gives 2 rounds,
proposals 1 gives 4 rounds

Read more: A7 chapter 21, an improver that tunes itself.

milestones.title: held-out meta-evaluation

functions.name: generalisation
functions.signature:
def generalisation(settings, train_score, held_score, shifted_score, start=DEFAULT,
seeds=FRESH_SEEDS, calls=CALLS):
functions.doc:
Run the improver `settings` once per seed using ONLY train_score, then re-score the
config it ends with on the other two scorers. Return a dict of means over the seeds:

    train    mean of (train_score(final) - train_score(start))
    held     mean of (held_score(final)  - held_score(start))
    shifted  mean of (shifted_score(final) - shifted_score(start))
    gap      train - held     (positive = the improver overfitted the training tasks)

milestones.task: Write generalisation(settings, train_score, held_score, shifted_score, start, seeds, calls). For each seed, run improve with the training scorer only. Compute each gain as the final config's score minus the start's score, under that scorer. Return a dict with the means under the keys train, held, shifted and gap.
milestones.checkpoint: check.py verifies: the four numbers against a reference on toy scorers (one where the held-out gain is negative). Then on the real scorers, from the naive config, that the training, held-out and shifted gains are all positive. And from the tuned config, that the gap is above 0.05 and the shifted gain is negative.
hints: Only train_score is ever passed to improve. The other two scorers are called on the final config only.
Each scorer is a function of a config. Subtract the start's score under the same scorer, not the training one.
Use rounds = calls // settings.proposals as in milestone 4.
milestones.solution:
def generalisation(settings, train_score, held_score, shifted_score,
                   start=DEFAULT, seeds=FRESH_SEEDS, calls=CALLS):
    """Train, held-out and shifted gains, and the gap."""
    rounds = calls // settings.proposals
    train, held, shifted = [], [], []
    for s in seeds:
        final, _ = improve(start, train_score, random.Random(s), rounds, settings)
        train.append(train_score(final) - train_score(start))
        held.append(held_score(final) - held_score(start))
        shifted.append(shifted_score(final) - shifted_score(start))
    mean = lambda xs: sum(xs) / len(xs)
    out = {"train": mean(train), "held": mean(held), "shifted": mean(shifted)}
    out["gap"] = out["train"] - out["held"]
    return out
milestones.explain:
Milestone 4 reported a win on the same tasks the improver used. That number is biased. The improver kept whichever settings looked best on three tasks and three random streams, so some of the gap is luck. This is the same selection effect that chapter 16 describes for programs. Here it happens one level up, and it has a name: meta-overfitting. The improver fits the training tasks instead of the problem.

To measure it, run the improver using only the training scorer. Then re-score the config it ends with on two other scorers. The held-out scorer uses six new tasks. The shifted scorer uses those same six tasks, but with item sizes 10 to 70 instead of 20 to 60. That tests a change in the kind of problem as well as a change in the instances. Report four numbers, each a mean over random streams: the training gain, the held-out gain, the shifted gain, and gap = train - held. A positive gap means the improver overfitted.

Two starting points tell different stories, and you should run both.

  • From the naive config the fix is structural: turn on a missing kind of edit. It works wherever the edit helps, so the gain should transfer.
  • From the tuned config nothing structural is missing. Any gain the improver finds comes from small differences that three training tasks happen to reward. Those should not transfer.
milestones.card:
A gain measured on the tasks an improver (a search over configs) used is biased: it kept whichever settings looked best there, so some of the gain is luck. One level up this is meta-overfitting: the improver fits its training tasks, not the problem. To measure it, run the improver on the training scorer only, then re-score the config it ends with on two scorers it never used: a held-out one with new tasks, and a shifted one with new tasks and a different range of item sizes.

For each seed s, run improve with train_score alone, random.Random(s) and calls // settings.proposals rounds. Each gain is a scorer's value for the final config minus its value for start. Return a dict of means over the seeds: train, held, shifted and gap, which is train - held. A positive gap means overfitting. A naive start config needs a structural fix that should transfer; a hand-tuned one does not, so its gains should not.

train gain +1.0, held-out gain +0.4: gap = 0.6
(illustrative numbers: the improver partly fitted its training tasks)

milestones.title: the audit

functions.name: audit
functions.doc:
Run `improver` under surveillance. Return (ok, reasons).

Snapshot BUDGET, TRAIN_TASKS and HELD_TASKS. Replace the module-level meta_utility by a
spy (a function with the same signature that records (task_seeds, budget) and then calls
the real one). Run improver(start, make_scorer(), random.Random(seed), rounds), then ALWAYS
(use try/finally) put the real meta_utility and the three constants back.
Reasons (strings, in this order, each at most once):
  "peeked"    some call used task seeds other than TRAIN_TASKS
  "budget"    some call used a budget other than the original BUDGET
  "tampered"  BUDGET, TRAIN_TASKS or HELD_TASKS differed after the run
ok is True when there are no reasons.

milestones.task: Write audit(improver, start=DEFAULT, rounds=2, seed=0). Snapshot BUDGET, TRAIN_TASKS and HELD_TASKS. Install a spy. Run improver(start, make_scorer(), random.Random(seed), rounds). In a finally block restore the real function and the constants. Return (ok, reasons), with reasons in the order "peeked", "budget", "tampered".
milestones.checkpoint: check.py verifies: the honest improver is accepted with no reasons; cheat_budget gives ["budget"]; cheat_peek gives ["peeked"]; cheat_tamper includes "tampered". A sneaky improver that builds a held-out scorer is still caught. An improver that does both gets the reasons in order. A crashing improver leaves nothing patched. And after all this the honest improver still gains on the training tasks.
hints: Declare global meta_utility, BUDGET, TRAIN_TASKS, HELD_TASKS. Assigning to meta_utility replaces the name that make_scorer looks up at call time.
The spy must have the same signature as meta_utility, including lo and hi defaults, and must return the real result.
Read the constants again after the run, but before restoring them, so you can compare. Compare tasks as tuples.
The cached scorer hides repeat calls on purpose. That is fine: a repeat of an honest call is honest.
milestones.solution:
def audit(improver, start=DEFAULT, rounds=2, seed=0):
    """Run `improver` under surveillance: (ok, reasons)."""
    global meta_utility, BUDGET, TRAIN_TASKS, HELD_TASKS
    real = meta_utility
    before = (BUDGET, TRAIN_TASKS, HELD_TASKS)
    calls = []

    def spy(config, task_seeds, budget, lo=20, hi=60):
        calls.append((tuple(task_seeds), budget))
        return real(config, task_seeds, budget, lo, hi)

    meta_utility = spy
    try:
        improver(start, make_scorer(), random.Random(seed), rounds)
        after = (BUDGET, TRAIN_TASKS, HELD_TASKS)
    finally:
        meta_utility = real
        BUDGET, TRAIN_TASKS, HELD_TASKS = before
    reasons = []
    if any(tasks != tuple(before[1]) for tasks, _ in calls):
        reasons.append("peeked")
    if any(b != before[0] for _, b in calls):
        reasons.append("budget")
    if after != before:
        reasons.append("tampered")
    return not reasons, reasons
milestones.explain:
Everything so far assumed an honest improver. Now suppose it can cheat. The improver is just a function that receives a scorer. In a single Python process it can also import the module and call meta_utility directly. Three cheats are given in the starter:

  • cheat_budget scores candidates with ten times the budget. Its configs look better because they were tested under a budget they will never get.
  • cheat_peek scores candidates on the held-out tasks. It then reports a held-out number it selected on.
  • cheat_tamper raises the module's BUDGET constant, then calls the honest scorer.

The defence is a tripwire. audit swaps the module's meta_utility for a spy that records the task seeds and the budget of each call and then calls the real one. It runs the improver, and it always restores everything in a finally block. A call on tasks other than the training tasks is "peeked". A call with a different budget is "budget". A changed constant afterwards is "tampered". Run the cheats and the honest improver side by side, starting from the naive config:

import random
import sys
sys.path.insert(0, ".")
import solution as lab

train = lab.make_scorer()
held = lab.make_scorer(lab.HELD_TASKS)
start = lab.DEFAULT
print(f"{'improver':13s} {'train':>7} {'held-out':>9}  audit")
for name, imp in (("honest", lab.honest()),
                  ("cheat_budget", lab.cheat_budget),
                  ("cheat_peek", lab.cheat_peek)):
    final = imp(start, train, random.Random(0), 4)
    gain_tr = train(final) - train(start)
    gain_he = held(final) - held(start)
    ok, why = lab.audit(imp, start)
    verdict = "accepted" if ok else "rejected " + str(why)
    print(f"{name:13s} {gain_tr:+7.3f} {gain_he:+9.3f}  {verdict}")

honest         +1.000    +1.056  accepted
cheat_budget   +1.000    +1.139  rejected ['budget']
cheat_peek     +1.000    +1.361  rejected ['peeked']

Look at what this shows. All three improvers gain the same on the training tasks. The cheat that peeks gets a better held-out number, +1.361 against +1.056, but only because it picked its config on those tasks. The budget cheat is also slightly ahead. Neither number is evidence of a better improver. The audit rejects both before anyone can quote them.

A tripwire is not a wall

This audit catches improvers that go through the module's meta_utility name. A determined cheater in the same process could rebind that name to its own function, read the call stack, or edit the spy. A real system puts the improver in a separate process that holds only a handle to the scorer, and keeps the held-out tasks on a machine the improver cannot reach. That is the point of chapter 16's rule that the evaluation set must be physically out of reach. The audit here shows what to look for. It does not prove an improver is honest.
